questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=(5y-7x+2)^{5}.
$$

Using a substitution of the form $z=5y-7x,$ transform the differential equation into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z).$ What is the function $f(z)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=5y-7x.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=5\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-7\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{5}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{7}{5}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{7}{5} & =(z+2)^{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z),$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=5(z+2)^{5}-7.
$$

Therefore, $f(z)=5(z+2)^{5}-7.$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x+2y+5}.
$$

Using a substitution of the form $z=x+2y,$ transform the differential equation into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z).$ What is the function $f(z)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+2y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+2\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{2} & ={e}^{z+5}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z),$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2{e}^{z+5}+1.
$$

Therefore, $f(z)=2{e}^{z+5}+1.$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={tan}^{2}⁡(3x-5y).
$$

Using a substitution of the form $z=3x-5y,$ transform the differential equation into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z).$ What is the function $f(z)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=3x-5y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=3-5\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{3}{5}-\frac{1}{5}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5}-\frac{1}{5}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & ={tan}^{2}⁡z\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z),$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=3-5{tan}^{2}⁡z.
$$

Therefore, $f(z)=3-5{tan}^{2}⁡z.$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={cos}^{2}⁡(2x-y+1).
$$

Using a substitution of the form $z=2x-y,$ transform the differential equation into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z).$ What is the function $f(z)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=2x-y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & ={cos}^{2}⁡(z+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z),$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2-{cos}^{2}⁡(z+1).
$$

Therefore, $f(z)=2-{cos}^{2}⁡(z+1).$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{e}^{2}}{(x+y)^{2}}.
$$

Using a substitution of the form $z=x+y,$ transform the differential equation into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z).$ What is the function $f(z)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & =\frac{{e}^{2}}{{z}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z),$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{e}^{2}}{{z}^{2}}+1.
$$

Therefore, $f(z)=\frac{{e}^{2}}{{z}^{2}}+1.$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\sqrt{x+y}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)}-1.
$$

 
The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=\frac{x}{2}+C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & =\frac{\sqrt{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡z}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\sqrt{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡z}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡z}{\sqrt{z}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡z}{\sqrt{z}}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Using integration by parts on the left side,

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡z & \,⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{z} \\ {v}^{′}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{z}} & \,⟹\,v=2\sqrt{z}\end{aligned}
$$

we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡z}{\sqrt{z}}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ 2\sqrt{z}\operatorname{ln}⁡z-2\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{z}}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ 2\sqrt{z}\operatorname{ln}⁡z-4\sqrt{z} & =x+K \\ 2\sqrt{z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡z-2) & =x+K \\ \sqrt{z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡z-2) & =\frac{x}{2}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=\frac{K}{2}.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{x+y}\,(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2) & =\frac{x}{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)=\sqrt{x+y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2).$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt{y+3x+2}-3.
$$

 
The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=x+C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=y+3x.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=3+\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-3.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-3 & =\sqrt{z+2}-3\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt{z+2}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{z+2}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int (z+2)^{-1/2}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ 2(z+2)^{1/2} & =x+C \\ 2\sqrt{z+2} & =x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{y+3x+2} & =x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)=2\sqrt{y+3x+2}.$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=3-{e}^{y-3x}.
$$

 
The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=x+C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=y-3x.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+3.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+3 & =3-{e}^{z}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{z}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-{e}^{-z}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ -\int {e}^{-z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ {e}^{-z} & =x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
{e}^{3x-y}=x+C
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)={e}^{3x-y}.$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{(x-2y)^{2}}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2y)}.
$$

 
The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=C-x,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=x-2y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1-2\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2}-\frac{{z}^{2}}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡z}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{z}^{2}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡z}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡z}{{z}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡z}{{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Using integration by parts on the left side,

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡z & \,⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{z} \\ {v}^{′}=\frac{1}{{z}^{2}} & \,⟹\,v=-\frac{1}{z}\end{aligned}
$$

we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡z}{{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ -\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡z}{z}+\int \frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ -\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡z}{z}-\frac{1}{z} & =x+C \\ -\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡z+1}{z} & =x+K \\ \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡z+1}{z} & =C-x,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-K.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2y)+1}{x-2y}=C-x
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2y)+1}{x-2y}.$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{(2x+y)\,{2}^{2x+y}}-2.
$$

 
The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡2+C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=2x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2 & =\frac{1}{z\,{2}^{z}}-2\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{z\,{2}^{z}}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z\,{2}^{z}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int z\,{2}^{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Using integration by parts on the left side,

$$
\begin{aligned}u=z & \,⟹\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}={2}^{z} & \,⟹\,v=\frac{{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\end{aligned}
$$

we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int z\,{2}^{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \frac{z\,{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int {2}^{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \frac{z\,{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(\frac{{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) & =x+C \\ \frac{{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(z-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) & =x+K \\ {2}^{z}(z-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡2+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=K\operatorname{ln}⁡2.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{2x+y}(2x+y-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡2+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)={2}^{2x+y}(2x+y-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}).$

canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \ln(x + y).
$$

Using a substitution of the form $z= x + y,$ transform the differential equation into an equation of the form $z'(x) = f(z).$ What is the function $f(z)?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z = x + y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}  = 1 + \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} - 1.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡z\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form $z'(x) = f(z),$ we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}  = \ln z+1.
$$

Therefore, $f(z) = \ln z + 1.$

canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = x + y.
$$

 
The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y) = x+C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z = x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}  = 1 + \,\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} - 1.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & =z\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form $z'(x) = f(z)$ gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}  = z+1.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{z+1}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int \frac{1}{z+1}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|z+1| & =x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\ln{|x+y+1|}  = x + C
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y) = \ln{|x+y+1|}.$
